Many women in business sell every day, their customers are happy, and yet at the end of the month there is no money to show for it. Usually the problem is not hard work. The problem is that the price was set by guessing, by copying the woman at the next stall, or by adding a little to the cost of ingredients only. This course teaches you to replace guessing with simple calculations that you can do with a pen, a notebook and the calculator on your phone.
Three words you will use in every lesson
list
**Revenue** (also called sales or turnover): all the money customers pay you. If you sell 40 bottles at ₦300 each, revenue is 40 x ₦300 = ₦12,000.
**Cost**: all the money the business spends to make and sell those goods, including things you pay for once a month, like rent and data.
**Profit**: what is left after all costs are taken away from revenue. Profit = Revenue minus Total cost. If the answer is negative, it is a loss.

Notice that profit is not the same as the money in your hand at the end of the day. Cash in hand includes money you will soon spend on the next bag of sugar, money a customer paid in advance, and sometimes money you borrowed. We will separate profit from cash properly in Module 3. For now, remember: **money in your purse is not automatically profit.**

Explain why mixed costs need to be split

To price well, you need to sort your costs in two different ways. Each way answers a different question. The first sorting asks: **can I trace this cost to one particular product?** The second asks: **does this cost go up and down when I make more or fewer items?** The same cost can be described both ways.
Direct and indirect costs
**Direct costs** can be traced to a single product or order. In tailoring, the lining, zip, buttons and thread used in one gown are direct costs of that gown.
**Indirect costs** (often called overheads) support the whole business and cannot be traced to one item. Shop rent, the apprentice's monthly stipend, generator fuel and phone data are indirect costs.
Fixed and variable costs
**Variable costs** rise and fall with how much you produce or sell. Make twice as many packs of chin-chin and you use about twice as much flour, oil and packaging.
**Fixed costs** stay about the same each month whether you sell a little or a lot, at least within your normal range of work. Rent, your own monthly wage, and a market levy are fixed costs.

**Mixed (semi-variable) costs** have a fixed part and a variable part. A generator may run every working day to light the shop (fixed part) and run longer in busy weeks (variable part). Estimate the two parts separately when you can.

Worked example: sorting Halima's tailoring costs for one month
For example, Halima runs a small tailoring shop in Kaduna. Customers bring their own fabric; she supplies lining and accessories. In a normal month she sews about 40 garments. Prices are approximate.
Direct materials for one gown: lining 2 yards at ₦1,500 = ₦3,000, zip ₦300, thread ₦200, interfacing ₦500, buttons ₦400. Total = 3,000 + 300 + 200 + 500 + 400 = ₦4,400 per gown.
These materials are direct and variable: 40 gowns x ₦4,400 = ₦176,000 a month if every garment were a gown like this.
Monthly indirect costs: rent ₦30,000, apprentice ₦20,000, generator fuel ₦24,000, phone data ₦6,000. Total = 30,000 + 20,000 + 24,000 + 6,000 = ₦80,000.
She treats these indirect costs as fixed, because they barely change between a quiet month and a busy month.
Indirect cost carried by each garment in a 40-garment month = ₦80,000 divided by 40 = ₦2,000.

Each gown carries ₦4,400 of direct materials plus ₦2,000 share of overheads, so ₦6,400 before Halima pays herself or makes any profit. If she charged ₦6,000 for sewing, she would be losing money on every gown.
Why the overhead share changes with volume

Look again at the ₦80,000 of fixed costs. In a slow month with only 20 garments, each garment must carry ₦80,000 divided by 20 = ₦4,000 of overhead. In a busy month of 50 garments, each carries ₦80,000 divided by 50 = ₦1,600. The variable cost per gown stays ₦4,400 either way. This is why busy months feel profitable and slow months hurt so much: **fixed costs do not shrink when sales fall.**
Equipment is a cost even after you have paid for it

A sealing machine bought for ₦72,000 that will last about 24 months costs the business roughly ₦72,000 divided by 24 = ₦3,000 a month. Accountants call this depreciation. Include it as a fixed cost so that your prices save up for the replacement.

Write your own monthly wage as a fixed cost, even if you only take it when sales are good. A price that does not cover your wage is subsidised by your unpaid time. If family members help without pay, estimate what you would pay a helper for those hours too, so the price still works on the day you hire someone.

Every calculation in this course is only as good as the numbers you put in. If your flour price is three months old, or you guess that a bag of sugar makes 'about ten batches' without checking, your price will be wrong. This lesson prepares the ground: records, measurements, a separate business account, and protection against the scams that target traders who receive transfers.
1. Capture every cost for at least two weeks
Keep every receipt in one envelope or snap a photo of it into a WhatsApp chat with yourself named 'Business costs'.
When there is no receipt (market purchases, okada fares), write the amount in your notebook the same day.
Note the quantity as well as the price: '10 kg flour, ₦15,000', not just '₦15,000'.
At the end of each week, copy the totals into your cost table from Lesson 1.2.
2. Measure, do not guess

Weigh a whole batch the first time you cost it. A kitchen scale that reads in grams is one of the best investments a food or cosmetics business can make. Count how many good units a batch really gives, after removing burnt, broken or misshapen ones. If a 50 kg bag of flour gives you exactly five 10 kg batches, write that down; do not rely on what the seller told you.

Worked example: turning a week of receipts into costs
For example, Ngozi fries and packs chin-chin in Owerri. She collected her receipts for one week in which she made 4 batches of 50 packs. Prices are approximate.
Flour: two purchases of 10 kg at ₦15,000 and one 20 kg purchase at ₦30,000. Total flour = 40 kg for ₦60,000, which is ₦15,000 per 10 kg batch.

She checks: 4 batches x 50 packs = 200 packs made. She found 6 broken or burnt packs, so she sold 194 good packs.
She writes all of this into her notebook with dates, and notes that wastage was 6 out of 200, which is 3 percent.
Ngozi now has real, dated costs per batch for her three biggest items and a measured wastage rate of 3 percent, ready for the unit cost calculation in Module 2.
3. Separate business money from household money

When sales money and housekeeping money sit in one purse or one account, you cannot tell whether the business is making profit. Open a separate account or wallet for the business. Many Nigerian banks and mobile money providers such as OPay and Moniepoint offer accounts you can open from your phone. Pay all business costs from it, receive all sales into it, and pay yourself a fixed wage from it into your personal account.

4. Protect your money from payment scams

**Fake credit alerts**: some fraudsters show a fake transfer screenshot or send an SMS that looks like a bank alert. Confirm every payment inside your bank or wallet app, or on your POS, before releasing goods.
**OTP and PIN requests**: no genuine bank, POS company or customer needs your PIN, password or one-time code. Never share them, even with someone claiming to be bank staff.
**Overpayment tricks**: a 'customer' sends too much and asks you to refund the extra. Wait until the full amount shows in your app and check it is not reversed.
**Supplier account changes**: if a supplier suddenly sends new account details, call them on the number you already have before paying.
Customer data is your responsibility

Customer phone numbers, addresses and payment details should be used only for their orders. Do not post order screenshots that show other people's numbers or addresses. Nigeria has a Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023), so treat personal data with care: share it only when needed and delete what you no longer need.
5. Decide your own wage now

Write a monthly amount you would accept to do this work for someone else. This is not a dream number; it is a fair wage for your hours. You will include it as a fixed cost in every calculation. If the business cannot yet pay it, the calculations will show you how many more sales or how much higher a price you need, which is far better than hiding the gap. Review the wage once a year, or sooner if prices in the market rise sharply.

Unit cost is what it costs you to produce and sell **one** item: one pack, one bottle, one gown, one hairdo. It has two parts. The **variable cost per unit** comes from the batch or job itself. The **fixed cost per unit** is your share of monthly overheads, spread across the number of units you expect to sell in a month. Add them and you have the **full cost per unit**, the lowest price at which you cover everything, including your own wage.
The four-step method
List every variable cost for one batch, with quantity and price.
Add them and divide by the number of good units the batch gives. This is variable cost per unit.
Add up all monthly fixed costs and divide by the number of units you realistically sell in a month. This is fixed cost per unit.
Add the two: full cost per unit = variable cost per unit + fixed cost per unit.

Step 3: choose a realistic monthly volume

The fixed cost per unit depends on the volume you divide by, so be honest. Use your average sales over the last two or three months, not your best month. If Ngozi used her best-ever month of 300 packs, she would get ₦110,000 divided by 300 = about ₦367 per pack, a full cost of about ₦1,307, and she would believe she is more profitable than she is. If you are just starting, use a careful estimate and recheck after the first month.
Adjusting for wastage

Burnt, broken or unsold items are not free. Their cost must be carried by the good units. The rule is simple: **divide the batch cost by the number of good units, not the number you planned.** If one of Ngozi's batches gives only 48 good packs instead of 50, her variable cost per good pack becomes ₦47,000 divided by 48 = about ₦979, roughly ₦39 more per pack. Over 200 packs a month that is close to ₦8,000 of hidden cost. Reducing wastage is often the cheapest way to increase profit.
Cost from the price you will pay next time

When prices are rising, use the price you will pay for your next purchase, not what you paid two months ago. Call or message your supplier before you recalculate. Write the date beside every price, and keep the old price too so you can see how fast costs are moving.
Unit cost for a service

If you sell a service, such as hair braiding, make-up or lessons, the 'unit' is one job or one hour. Variable costs are the materials used on that job (attachment hair, gel, products) plus any helper paid per job. Fixed costs per job are your monthly overheads divided by the number of jobs you do in a typical month. Your time is usually the biggest cost, so make sure your wage is in the fixed costs.
Rounding
Work in whole naira and round unit costs up, not down. Rounding up protects your profit; rounding down quietly gives it away.

Full cost per unit is useful, but it changes every time your sales volume changes. Break-even analysis gives you a steadier way to think. It answers the question every business owner asks: **how many do I need to sell each month before I start making money?**
Contribution margin

Each sale brings in the selling price. Part of that money immediately pays for the variable cost of the item. What is left over is the **contribution margin**: it contributes first to paying fixed costs, and once those are covered, it becomes profit.
**Contribution margin per unit** = Selling price minus Variable cost per unit.
**Contribution margin ratio** = Contribution margin per unit divided by Selling price. It tells you how many kobo of every naira of sales are left to cover fixed costs and profit.
**Break-even point in units** = Total monthly fixed costs divided by Contribution margin per unit. Always round **up** to the next whole unit.
**Break-even sales in naira** = Break-even units x Selling price (or Fixed costs divided by Contribution margin ratio).

Worked example: Ngozi's break-even at ₦1,500 a pack
For example, Ngozi's variable cost is ₦940 a pack and her fixed costs are ₦110,000 a month (from Lesson 2.1). She currently sells at ₦1,500.
Contribution margin per pack = ₦1,500 minus ₦940 = ₦560.
Contribution margin ratio = 560 divided by 1,500 = 0.373, about 37 percent.
Break-even units = ₦110,000 divided by ₦560 = 196.4. Round up: 197 packs.
Check: 197 x ₦560 = ₦110,320, which covers ₦110,000. At 196 packs she would have only ₦109,760, which is short.
Break-even sales in naira = 197 x ₦1,500 = ₦295,500.
Ngozi must sell 197 packs, about ₦295,500 of sales, every month just to cover her costs including her wage. Only the 198th pack onwards gives profit, ₦560 each.

Margin of safety

The **margin of safety** is how far your sales can fall before you hit break-even. Margin of safety = Expected sales minus Break-even sales. If Ngozi expects to sell 250 packs, her margin of safety is 250 minus 197 = 53 packs. As a percentage: 53 divided by 250 = about 21 percent. A thin margin of safety, below about 10 percent, means one bad week could push the month into a loss.
Using break-even to test a new price

Suppose Ngozi raises her price to ₦1,700. Her variable cost stays ₦940, so contribution becomes ₦1,700 minus ₦940 = ₦760 a pack. Break-even = ₦110,000 divided by ₦760 = 144.7, rounded up to 145 packs (check: 145 x 760 = ₦110,200). A ₦200 price rise cuts the packs she needs to break even from 197 to 145, a drop of 52 packs a month. She must judge whether customers will accept ₦1,700; if most still buy, the business becomes much safer.

Never sell below variable cost

If a price is lower than the variable cost, each sale loses money before rent or wages are even considered. For Ngozi, any price under ₦940 makes every extra pack a direct loss. Clearance of stock about to spoil is the only usual exception.
Worked example: break-even for a braiding service
For example, Zainab braids knotless braids from a rented chair in a salon in Abuja and charges ₦12,000 per head. Prices are approximate.
Variable cost per head: attachment hair ₦3,500, gel and mousse ₦500, assistant paid ₦1,000 per head. Total = ₦5,000.
Contribution per head = ₦12,000 minus ₦5,000 = ₦7,000.
Monthly fixed costs: chair rent ₦20,000, her own wage ₦50,000, data ₦5,000, share of power ₦15,000. Total = ₦90,000.
Break-even = ₦90,000 divided by ₦7,000 = 12.9, rounded up to 13 heads. Check: 13 x 7,000 = ₦91,000.
Zainab needs 13 clients a month, roughly three a week, to cover all costs including her wage. Every client after that adds ₦7,000 of profit.
What break-even assumes

The calculation assumes one price, one variable cost and that everything you make is sold. Real life is messier. If you sell several products, work out break-even for your main product first, or use an average contribution per sale from your records. If you discount often, use your average actual selling price, not the price on the label.

You now know your full cost and your break-even point. The next step is choosing a selling price. Most small businesses use **cost-plus pricing**: start from cost and add a profit. There are two ways to add it, and confusing them is one of the most common and costly mistakes in small business.
Markup and margin are not the same
**Markup** is profit as a percentage of **cost**. Price = Cost x (1 + markup). A ₦1,000 item with 50 percent markup sells for ₦1,500.
**Margin** is profit as a percentage of **selling price**. Price = Cost divided by (1 minus margin). A ₦1,000 item with 50 percent margin sells for ₦1,000 divided by 0.5 = ₦2,000.
The same ₦500 profit on a ₦1,500 price is a 50 percent markup but only a 33 percent margin (500 divided by 1,500).

Two other ways to think about price
**Competitor-based pricing**: you set your price near what similar sellers charge. It is quick, but only safe if your own cost is lower than that price.

**Value-based pricing**: you price by what the product is worth to the customer, for example a cake for a wedding, a rush tailoring job or delivery to the office. Customers often pay more for speed, reliability, quality and convenience. Your cost is still the floor.

Break-even tells you how to stop losing money. A **profit target** tells you how to make the money you actually want. The method is a small extension of the break-even formula: you simply add the profit you want to the fixed costs before dividing.

Choose a target based on what the profit must pay for, not a round number that sounds nice. Profit is the money that buys a new fryer or sewing machine, builds an emergency buffer, repays a loan, and lets the business grow. Your wage is already in fixed costs, so the target is money for the business itself. Start with a modest figure, reach it for two or three months, then raise it.

Units needed for target profit = (Monthly fixed costs + Target profit) divided by Contribution margin per unit. Round up to the next whole unit.

**Equals gross profit.**
**Minus operating expenses**: your fixed costs, such as rent, your wage, data, levies and equipment wear.
**Equals net profit** (or net loss).

Profit is a measure of whether the business is earning more than it spends over a period. **Cash flow** is the actual movement of money in and out of your account or purse. A business can show a healthy profit and still be unable to buy flour on Monday. Many small businesses fail not because they are unprofitable, but because they run out of cash.
Why profit and cash differ
**Credit sales**: counted as sales in the P&L, but no cash arrives until the customer pays.
**Unsold stock**: you paid cash to make it, but it is not yet a cost in the P&L.
**Equipment wear (depreciation)**: a cost in the P&L, but no cash leaves this month.
**Loan repayments**: cash leaves, but repaying the loan amount is not an expense in the P&L (interest is).
**Advance payments and deposits**: cash arrives before the sale is completed.
Worked example: Ngozi's profit was ₦115,200, so where is the cash?
For example, take Ngozi's month from Lesson 3.2. She started with ₦40,000 in her business account. She also repaid ₦30,000 of a loan during the month.
Cash in: retail sales ₦442,000. The supermarket's ₦84,000 is not due until next month. Cash in = ₦442,000.
Cash out: 7 batches made at ₦47,000 each = ₦329,000. Fixed costs paid in cash = ₦110,000 minus ₦3,000 equipment wear = ₦107,000. Loan repayment ₦30,000. Cash out = ₦466,000.
Net cash flow = ₦442,000 minus ₦466,000 = minus ₦24,000. Closing cash = ₦40,000 minus ₦24,000 = ₦16,000.
Reconcile: profit ₦115,200 + equipment wear ₦3,000 minus unpaid credit sale ₦84,000 minus unsold stock ₦28,200 minus loan repayment ₦30,000 = minus ₦24,000. It matches.
Ngozi earned ₦115,200 profit, yet her cash fell to ₦16,000, not enough to pay for even one ₦47,000 batch. Until the supermarket pays, she cannot keep production going without help.

Controlling credit and money risks
Take a deposit, for example 50 percent, before starting custom orders such as cakes, outfits or event packs.
Give credit only to known customers, write the amount and due date, and send a polite WhatsApp reminder on the due date.
Keep a cash buffer, ideally at least one month of fixed costs, before taking big credit orders.
Do not borrow to cover a business that is losing money; fix the price or costs first.
Be wary of 'investment' offers that promise high monthly returns with little risk; schemes like this have collapsed and taken traders' savings.
Ways to speed up your cash
Agree shorter payment terms with wholesale buyers, for example 14 days instead of 30, or a small discount for paying on delivery.
Buy perishable materials close to production day rather than weeks ahead.
Produce to match sales, so less cash sits in unsold stock.
Clear slow-moving stock early, at a price still above variable cost.

Common gaps in first plans
Fixed costs listed without the owner's wage, so the plan looks profitable when it is not.
A volume taken from the best month ever instead of an average month.
A break-even point above what the business can actually produce in a month.
No plan for the cash needed before the first customers pay.
Old supplier prices with no dates beside them.

If you sell several products, build the plan around your two or three best sellers. Calculate contribution for each, then use your expected sales mix to find an average contribution per sale, as Ngozi did with retail and wholesale in Lesson 3.2. Keep small, occasional products out of the plan until they sell regularly.

Knowing your numbers gives you confidence, but customers do not buy numbers. They buy quality, freshness, reliability and convenience. This lesson shows you how to talk about value, why discounts are expensive, and how to raise a price when costs go up without losing your loyal customers.
Talk about value, not cost
Name the benefit: 'fried fresh every Tuesday and Friday', 'sealed pack, stays crunchy for weeks', 'full 250 g, weighed on a scale'.
Show proof: photos of your clean kitchen or workshop, a short video on WhatsApp Status, reviews from real customers who agree to be quoted.
Explain what is included: delivery within your area, fittings, adjustments, gift packaging.
Never apologise for your price. Say it clearly and wait.
The real cost of a discount

A discount comes straight out of your contribution, not out of your price. A 10 percent cut in price can remove a much bigger share of the money that pays your fixed costs and profit. Before you agree to any discount, calculate how many more units you must sell to end up with the same total contribution.
Worked example: what 10 percent off costs Ngozi
For example, Ngozi sells 200 packs a month at ₦1,700 with a variable cost of ₦940. A customer suggests a 10 percent 'promo' price.
Current contribution = ₦1,700 minus ₦940 = ₦760 a pack. Total = 200 x ₦760 = ₦152,000.
Discounted price = ₦1,700 minus 10 percent (₦170) = ₦1,530. New contribution = ₦1,530 minus ₦940 = ₦590 a pack.
Packs needed for the same ₦152,000 = ₦152,000 divided by ₦590 = 257.6, rounded up to 258 packs.
Extra packs needed = 258 minus 200 = 58, which is 29 percent more sales, more frying and more stock.

A 10 percent price cut needs 29 percent more sales just to stand still. Ngozi offers a bundle instead: 5 packs for ₦8,000. Contribution on the bundle = ₦8,000 minus (5 x ₦940 = ₦4,700) = ₦3,300, or ₦660 a pack, and each sale is five packs.

Needs many more sales

Before discounting, look for a way to give more value while keeping your price.

When a customer says 'it is too expensive'
Stay calm and ask what she is comparing with. Sometimes the other product is smaller or lower quality.
Restate the value: weight, freshness, finishing, delivery, after-sales adjustments.
Offer a choice instead of a cut: a smaller size, a bundle, or a simpler version at a lower price that still covers your costs.
If she still wants a lower price than your variable cost allows, thank her and let the sale go. Not every sale is a good sale.
When costs rise: recalculate, then decide
Worked example: flour goes up 20 percent
For example, Ngozi's flour price rises from ₦15,000 to ₦18,000 for 10 kg. Everything else stays the same.
Extra cost per batch = ₦18,000 minus ₦15,000 = ₦3,000. Per pack = ₦3,000 divided by 50 = ₦60.
New variable cost = ₦940 + ₦60 = ₦1,000 a pack.
If she keeps ₦1,700, contribution falls to ₦700 and break-even rises from 145 to ₦110,000 divided by ₦700 = 157.1, so 158 packs.
To keep her ₦760 contribution she needs ₦1,000 + ₦760 = ₦1,760. She rounds to ₦1,800, giving ₦800 contribution.
Ngozi raises her price to ₦1,800 with two weeks' notice. Her contribution is protected and break-even drops to ₦110,000 divided by ₦800 = 137.5, so 138 packs.
How to announce a price change
Give notice, for example one or two weeks, so regular customers can stock up at the old price.
Explain the reason in one honest sentence, such as higher flour and oil prices.
Remind them of the value they get: same weight, same freshness, same delivery.
Thank them, and keep the message short and warm.
A sample WhatsApp message

Good afternoon, and thank you for buying from us. Because flour and oil prices have gone up, our 250 g chin-chin will be ₦1,800 from Monday 1st. It is still freshly fried twice a week, sealed and full weight. Orders placed before Sunday stay at ₦1,700. Thank you for your support.

Wholesale customers need more notice than retail customers because they have printed their own price lists. Tell them about a month ahead if you can, and recalculate your wholesale price with the same method so that it stays well above your new variable cost.
Do not shrink the pack quietly
Reducing the weight while keeping the label and price the same is dishonest and customers notice. If you change the size, change the label and tell customers.

What-if planning

Before you change a price, take a bigger shop, or accept a large order, test the effect on paper. Use one simple formula: **Profit = Units sold x Contribution per unit minus Fixed costs.** Change one number at a time and see what happens to profit.
Worked example: Ngozi tests five scenarios
For example, Ngozi's base month: 250 packs at ₦1,700, variable cost ₦940 (contribution ₦760), fixed costs ₦110,000. Base profit = 250 x 760 = ₦190,000, minus ₦110,000 = ₦80,000.
Variable cost up 10 percent to ₦1,034: contribution ₦666. Profit = 250 x 666 = ₦166,500 minus ₦110,000 = ₦56,500.
Sales fall 20 percent to 200 packs: profit = 200 x 760 = ₦152,000 minus ₦110,000 = ₦42,000.
Rent goes up, adding ₦20,000 to fixed costs: profit = ₦190,000 minus ₦130,000 = ₦60,000.

A ₦100 price rise adds ₦25,000 profit, while a 20 percent drop in sales removes ₦38,000. Ngozi now knows that protecting sales volume and price matters most, and that a 10 percent cost rise must be passed on quickly.

What-if for a big order

Suppose a supermarket offers Ngozi a regular order of 300 packs a month at ₦1,300, paid 30 days after delivery. Contribution = ₦1,300 minus ₦940 = ₦360 a pack, so 300 x ₦360 = ₦108,000 extra contribution a month, with no extra fixed costs if her kitchen and helper can cope. But 300 packs means 6 extra batches, so her capacity must double, and 6 x ₦47,000 = ₦282,000 of cash is tied up for a month before the first payment arrives. The order looks profitable on paper; the real questions are capacity and cash.
Signs it is time to re-price
Gross margin has fallen for two months in a row.
A main input such as flour, oil, fabric or packaging has risen by more than about 10 percent.
You are always sold out early, which suggests customers value the product more than your price shows.
Your fixed costs have changed, such as new rent or a new helper.
